title: SRE documentation standards: SLOs, error budgets, capacity planning, and runbooks
author: Ari Chen
summary: Standardized guidance for SRE documentation at Redwood Inference covering SLO and error budget definitions, capacity planning cadence, reliability initiatives, incident review standards, runbook templates, and operational tooling ownership.
body:
Purpose:
Provide a single, company-wide standard for SRE documentation so service owners, SREs, and platform engineers can create consistent, auditable artifacts that drive reliability and predictable operations. This doc covers minimum content required for SLOs and error budgets, capacity planning, reliability initiatives, incident review expectations, runbook format and lifecycle, and recommended tooling integrations.

Scope:
- All customer-facing and internal low-latency services that are part of Redwood’s inference platform (hosted API, dedicated pools, private deployments, control plane services).
- Applies to service owners, SREs, on-call engineers, and product owners.

1) SLOs and error budgets
Overview:
- Every service must publish at least one Service Level Objective (SLO) tied to customer-facing behaviour (latency, availability, or correctness) and an associated error budget policy.
- SLOs should reflect user impact and be measurable from production telemetry (Datadog, Prometheus, internal tracing).

Required fields for an SLO document:
1. SLO name and short description.
2. Owner (service owner + primary SRE).
3. Stakeholders (product, infra, and security contacts).
4. Metric definition (including metric name, aggregation, rollup, and query example).
5. SLO target and time window (e.g., 99.9% successful requests over a 30-day rolling window).
6. Error budget calculation and current burn rate dashboard link.
7. Measurement method and alerting thresholds.
8. Error budget policy: escalation actions when burn rate exceeds thresholds.
9. Related runbooks and playbooks.

SLO example (text table):
- SLO name: Hosted API P95 latency (text-generation)
- Description: P95 request latency for text-generation endpoints measured at edge proxies excluding cached responses.
- Owner: ML Platform (service-owner@redwood.com); Primary SRE: ari.chen@redwood.com
- Metric query (PromQL): sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{route=~"/v1/generate.*",env="prod"}[5m])) by (le) -> histogram_quantile(0.95, ... )
- Target: P95 <= 250ms over 30 days
- Error budget: 100% - SLO -> allowable 0.1% of requests failing the latency requirement
- Burn policy:
  - Burn rate > 1.5x for 6 hours: notify product + infra, pause nonessential rollouts
  - Burn rate > 3x for 1 hour: page on-call SRE and escalate to on-call manager

Error budget governance:
- Weekly SLO review in SRE triage meeting.
- If error budget is exhausted for a service for more than 24 hours, a reliability initiative must be opened and prioritized with product.
- Quarterly SLO alignment: product and SRE review to adjust targets or measurement gaps.

2) Capacity planning
Goals:
- Ensure sufficient headroom to meet SLOs during expected peak traffic and planned growth.
- Surface capacity risks early and align with finance and procurement for committed capacity (Dedicated) purchases.

Cadence and artifacts:
- Monthly capacity snapshot: current utilization, projected growth (next 90 days), scheduled deployments/rollouts, and known capacity reservations.
- Quarterly capacity review: cross-team review for burst and reserve strategy, autoscaling policy effectiveness, and spot instance exposure.
- Runbook: capacity-failure playbook (see Runbook templates section).

Minimum capacity plan contents:
- Service name, owner, and downstream dependencies.
- Current steady-state RPS and 95th/99th percentile token throughput per second.
- Baseline GPU/CPU/memory utilization per model variant and quantization profile.
- Autoscaling policies and cooldown windows.
- Planned events (model rollouts, marketing campaigns, third-party integrations) that affect traffic.
- Reserve/burst strategy and lead times for adding reserved capacity.

Capacity modeling example (text):
- Expected 30% growth over 90 days.
- Current GPU pool: 40 T4 equivalents, avg utilization 68% at P95 load.
- Target headroom: 25% buffer at P95 -> need +10 T4 equivalents in 60 days or enable burst policy to private cloud region.

3) Reliability initiatives
Definition:
- A reliability initiative is a time-boxed program (typically 2-8 weeks) to address a systemic reliability problem (high burn rate, frequent incidents, capacity constraint).

Initiative template (required fields):
- Title and short summary.
- Owner (product + SRE lead).
- Success criteria (measurable, tied to SLOs or incident reduction).
- Start and end dates.
- Key milestones and checkpoints.
- Resource allocation (headcount or budget).

Prioritization and lifecycle:
- Initiatives triggered automatically when a service exhausts an error budget for 7 consecutive days, or after two Sev2 incidents in a 30-day window.
- Initiatives must be included in the product roadmap and get a dedicated slot in the next sprint cycle unless waived by the CTO.

4) Incident review and postmortem standards
Scope:
- All Sev1 and Sev2 incidents must have a post-incident review (PIR) document created within 72 hours of mitigation.
- Sev3 with user impact or repeat occurrences may also require PIR at the on-call manager's discretion.

Postmortem required sections:
1. Executive summary (1-3 sentences).
2. Timeline of events (UTC timestamps).
3. Impact summary (services affected, customers, duration, severity).
4. Root cause analysis (technical cause + contributing factors).
5. Corrective actions (short-term mitigations and long-term fixes).
6. Action owners and due dates.
7. Follow-ups and closure criteria (linked to reliability initiative if applicable).
8. Blameless analysis notes (focus on system factors).

Review process:
- PIR draft assigned to incident commander.
- Peer review by at least two engineers (one SRE and one service owner).
- Postmortem review meeting within 7 days; meeting notes and decisions recorded in the postmortem doc.
- If corrective actions are not completed within 30 days, the owner must report status weekly to SRE leadership.

5) Operational tooling and telemetry standards
Minimum telemetry requirements:
- Traces: end-to-end distributed tracing for critical request paths (Zipkin/OpenTelemetry) with sampling that preserves tail-latency signals.
- Metrics: request count, success rate, latency distributions, queue depths, GPU utilization, cache hit ratios.
- Logs: structured logs with request id, service, route, model_version, and error codes.
- Dashboards: per-service SLO dashboard (SLO health, burn rate, latency histogram) and paged alert dashboard.

Alerting standards:
- Alerts should signal actionable conditions with runbooks linked. Examples: SLO burn rate > 2x for 30 min, queue backlog > threshold for 15 min, autoscaler failing to scale for 10 min.
- Use a three-tier alerting strategy: Info (email/slack), Warning (on-call notification), Critical (pager).

Tooling ownership and integrations:
- Observability: Datadog for metrics + dashboards; Tempo/Jaeger for traces; Loki for logs.
- Incident management: PagerDuty for on-call routing; Jira for action tracking; Confluence for documentation.
- Capacity and cost: Internal cost dashboard + tagging standards in cloud accounts.

6) Runbook standards and templates
Purpose:
- Runbooks must allow an on-call engineer to recover a service or mitigate customer-impacting conditions quickly and safely.

Runbook lifecycle:
- Authoring: service owner writes initial runbook during onboarding.
- Review: SRE reviews and approves prior to production launch.
- Maintenance: runbook owner must review every 90 days and after any related incident.

Runbook template (plain text sections):
- Title and short description
- Service owners and SRE contacts
- Pager routing and escalation policy
- Symptoms and how to verify impact
- Immediate mitigation steps (step-by-step, CLI/commands, and safe flags)
- Diagnosis steps and data sources (queries, dashboards, common trace patterns)
- Recovery steps and verification checklist
- Post-incident actions and links to PIR template
- Last reviewed and changelog

Runbook example excerpt (Immediate mitigation):
1. Confirm the service is unhealthy: curl -sSf "https://internal-api.prod/service/health" || true
2. If autoscaler failed, manually scale deployment: kubectl scale deployment svc-gen --replicas=5 -n prod
3. If queue backlog > 1000: pause non-critical ingestion jobs: POST https://ops-api/pause-ingestion
4. If model KV-cache thrashing suspected: roll back to previous model variant: kubectl set image deployment/svc-gen model-container=model:v1.3.4 -n prod

7) Documentation QA and audits
- Every SRE doc (SLOs, capacity plan, runbook, PIRs) must include metadata headers (owner, created_at, last_updated, reviewers) aligned with this template.
- The SRE team will run a quarterly documentation audit: each service must have an up-to-date SLO, capacity plan, and runbook. Non-compliant services are flagged and prioritized in the next reliability initiative.

8) Ownership and escalation matrix
- Service owner: owns product-level decisions and roadmaps.
- Primary SRE: owns operational readiness, runbooks, and on-call rotations.
- Platform SRE: owns shared tooling and capacity pool policies.
- On-call escalation: primary on-call -> on-call manager -> SRE director -> CTO (for extended outages > 8 hours or large customer impact).

Appendix: quick references
- Postmortem template link: /confluence/eng-sre/postmortem-template
- Runbook template link: /confluence/eng-sre/runbook-template
- SLO dashboard example: internal-dashboards://slo-hosted-api-p95
- Incident severity definitions: Sev1 = platform down or data loss; Sev2 = degraded customer experience; Sev3 = limited impact or internal-only issue.
